_comment: FINAL Assamese tokenizer (Model L). Trained on the FULL training split only, never on validation or test, so held-out fertility and Phase 2 perplexity are not optimistically biased.
_choice: 8,000 pieces, chosen from a 6k/8k/10k/12k sweep measured on held-out validation text. See _why_8000 below.
_why_8000: The vocabulary is not free: at d_model=384 with a tied output head it
costs vocab x 384 parameters out of the ~25M Phase 2 budget, and each
Transformer block costs 12 x 384^2 = 1,769,472. Vocabulary is therefore
bought directly out of depth, and depth is what Phase 3's comparative
reasoning needs.
Measured on held-out validation text (518.5M-token corpus, 2,416
Internet Archive books included):
vocab  chars/tok  fertility  unk rate  vocab used  embedding  layers
8,000 is the elbow, and the argument is a step function rather than a
smooth trade. 6k and 8k both afford twelve layers; 10k and 12k afford
eleven. Within twelve layers, 8k strictly dominates 6k -- 4.7% better
compression, higher vocabulary utilisation, same depth -- so 8k is the
best tokenizer available at no cost in layers. Going further to 10k buys
3.3% fertility for a whole Transformer block, and 12k buys 2.5% more for
19% of the model spent on a lookup table that performs no computation.
Unknown-token rate is 0.000% at every candidate, so it cannot
discriminate here; byte_fallback covers the tail. The decision rests on
fertility and compression against parameter cost, as the assignment asks.
Vocabulary utilisation RISES with size across the whole sweep (97.02% ->
98.39%), which normally indicates the corpus could support more pieces
still. It is not taken as an argument for a larger vocabulary here: the
binding constraint is the parameter budget, not whether the corpus can
fill the vocabulary.
10,000 is retained as a documented alternative should Phase 2 find the
twelfth layer worth less than the compression.
_supersedes: An earlier configuration chose 16,000 on a sweep over 4k-32k. Two things
invalidated it. The corpus grew from 289M to 518.5M tokens when the
Internet Archive collection was repaired, so the old sweep measured a
different distribution. And the selection ignored the parameter budget:
16,000 spends 6,144,000 parameters, 30% of the model, leaving ten layers.
The sweep bracket was moved to 6k-12k for both languages accordingly.
_max_sentence_length_note: SentencePiece's limit is in BYTES and defaults to 4,192. The Bengali-Assamese block costs three bytes per character, so the exporter's 2,000-character chunks reach ~6,000 bytes and would be dropped SILENTLY. Measured on Telugu, the default discarded 0.72% of lines but 7.15% of the text, weighted towards the longest continuous prose - exactly what subword learning depends on.
_input_sentence_size_note: Sentences SentencePiece loads into memory, sampled with shuffle_input_sentence across the whole export. Not a corpus limit: sample_rate is 1.0, so every document in the training split contributes lines.
_train_extremely_large_corpus_note: Memory-frugal training path. The training split is now 1.77B characters, up from 1.09B, and the earlier 10%-sample sweep already produced std::bad_alloc at 48k on this machine. Slower, but it finishes.
